thread.title_full: Wildfires prompt evacuations across Washington state. Here's how to prepare - NewsBreak

author: Karlee Van De Venter
title: Wildfires prompt evacuations across Washington state. Here's how to prepare - NewsBreak
text:
By Karlee Van De Venter ,
9 hours ago A long line of flames from a brush fire light up the night sky in Kennewick as firefighters work to prevent their advance toward houses in the Inspiration Estates housing development. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com Multiple wildfires have recently threatened residential areas across Washington state.
In Okanogan County, the Kaiser Canyon Fire and Sinlahekin Fire have collectively scorched nearly 130,000 acres.
The town of White Swan saw damage to multiple homes due to the Signal Peak and Ransier Fires, which together have torched nearly 4,000 acres.
Over the past week, evacuation orders have been issued in the town of White Swan and a section of Okanogan County . Meanwhile, residents in one Kennewick neighborhood were told to evacuate due to a wind-driven wildfire.
While no one wants to be forced to leave their home, it’s important to know wildfire evacuation protocols while living in fire-prone areas of Washington state.
Here’s what to know:
What should I put in my evacuation go-bag? You should prepare for evacuations before they happen.
Make plans with members of your household for different evacuation scenarios.
According to the Washington State Department of Natural Resources’ Wildfire Action Plan , you should focus on the “six P’s” when creating a go bag to have ready in case of a fire emergency:
People and pets Paper, phone numbers and important documents Prescriptions, vitamins and glasses Pictures and irreplaceable memorabilia Personal computer hard drive and disks Plastic (credit, debit, ATM cards) and cash If you’re prepared ahead of time, you can ensure the most complete go bag for emergency scenarios.
The California Department of Forestry & Fire Protection’s Ready For Wildfire website recommends including these items:
Face masks or coverings for smoke A three-day supply of nonperishable food (including pet food) Three gallons of water per person, with additional three-day supply for any pets Map with evacuation routes Prescriptions and special medications Change of clothes Extra glasses and contact lenses Extra set of car keys, credit cards, cash or traveler’s checks First aid kit Flashlight Battery-powered radio, extra batteries Sanitation supplies Copies of important documents Family photos and easy-to-carry valuables If it’s possible an evacuation will be ordered overnight, keep a flashlight and sturdy shoes near your bed. If time permits, grab small valuables, family photos and chargers.
When leaving your home under an evacuation order, cover up to protect yourself. Check the fire’s proximity and if necessary, wear long clothing and cover exposed skin.
If you don’t have a go bag prepared in advance, focus on irreplaceable items that can be easily carried, as well as pets and absolute necessities.
How do fire evacuation levels work in Washington state? Most counties in Washington state use the Ready, Set, Go evacuation level system . The only exceptions are Clallam and Wahkiakum counties, who use their own emergency management plans.
The Ready, Set, Go system has three evacuation levels: One for ready, two for set, and three for go.
Here’s how it works
Level One: Ready A level one evacuation notice is a warning to residents that there is danger in their area.
If you are in a level one evacuation area, you should assemble your go bag and coordinate a household plan. If you’ve already taken these steps, ensure everything is ready to go.
You should also frequently check for updates from local agencies and media.
While you do not have to evacuate at this time, anyone who is extra sensitive to smoke or has special needs should consider leaving early. Pet owners may also want to start leaving at this level.
Level Two: Set A level two evacuation notice means there is significant danger in your area. You should have your go bag on hand and look for updates on temporary shelters, which are typically available at this stage.
Most households should be getting out of the evacuation area during this level. If you choose to wait out a level two notice, you should be ready to evacuate at a moment’s notice.
Level Three: Go A level three evacuation notice is an order to leave your home immediately due to imminent threat.
If you have not gathered personal items or property at this point, don’t. Instead, leave as soon as possible.
Emergency services may not be able to help residents who do not evacuate at level three.
What is the difference between controlled and contained fires? When monitoring for updates on nearby wildfires, it’s important to know the terminology.
Fire crews will provide updates on how controlled or contained a fire is — but what is the difference between the two?
A fire’s containment level refers to its perimeter, according to the National Wildfire Coordinating Group .
Responding firefighters work to implement control lines, which are man-made barriers that cannot catch fire. This can mean removing all burnable material, digging a pit or taking other measures to prevent further spread.
Sometimes, controlled fires can be set around the existing perimeter, which keeps the wildfire from extending beyond those lines.
Once firefighters are confident the blaze will not grow past the barrier in place, barring a significantly large gust of wind or other severe complication, a control line is considered effective.
The percentage of containment reflects how much of a fire’s perimeter has effective control lines in place.
Once a fire is completely contained, it won’t have anywhere to spread. At that point, fire crews work to extinguish the remaining flames.
A fire is considered controlled when it has burned out or is mostly extinguished. It may have hot spots or embers still, but is no longer considered a public safety issue.
When there are no further signs of smoke or fire activity, a fire is considered fully out.
This story contains information from previous articles originally published in August 2023 , March 2025 and July 2025 . Becca Most and Shaun Goodwin contributed to the original reporting.
